maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Prime Minister whether, if two or more provinces do not join the plan, his determination is equally certain.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman's hypothetical question does not affect our determination to proceed with this matter.

speechtext:
In
welcoming the Prime Minister's statement that the government will proceed with the Canada pension plan, may I ask him this. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: I certainly hope the Prime Minister's statement proves to be true. But does he not take the statement by the premier of Ontario as indicating that Ontario may follow the course proposed by the province of Quebec?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman would like to take it as notice and deal with it when he makes his full statement on Monday. My question is, will the third level of government be included in such consultations?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext:
In federal-provincial committees and meetings of the kind to which the hon. member has referred it has been the custom in the past and, I think, the constitutionally appropriate custom, to have the municipalities represented by the provinces to which they are responsible. If there is to be any change in this constitutional procedure,
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)

that change would have to be made by agreement with the provinces. Indeed, I think it would have to be initiated by the provincial governments.

speechtext:

Be that as it may, I merely say we would like to give further thought to this question before making a statement.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

He is waiting to hear from us as to the nature of the committee and the kind of representation, and he has informed us, as he informed the press conference yesterday, that he would then decide whether Quebec would actually participate in the representation on the committee.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext:

There were reports coming from the federal-provincial conference to the effect that the federal government would transfer a larger share of direct taxation to the provinces. Could the Prime [DOT] Minister tell us whether that policy would apply only to provinces not taking part in the health insurance program or to all provinces?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there would be no distinction made with regard to any province in this matter.

speechtext:

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is a matter of government policy. No consideration has been given to it and no consideration can be given to it, of course, until we find out what the plans of the government of Quebec are.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has just made a summary statement,
Inquiries of the Ministry and in that connection I ask him this question. Is it the opinion of the government, received from the law officers of the crown, that the system of loans proposed in the speech from the throne is entirely within the competence of the federal parliament?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have just said that, and I am glad to repeat that we think this is within the competence of the federal parliament, particularly in view of the procedure we intend to propose whereby these loans will be made to individuals through the banks with the federal government guaranteeing the banks.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE
speechtext: That is not the question I asked the minister. Would this be a condition which the federal government would impose upon granting them an abatement of personal income tax? Would this be done only if they were willing to continue reciprocity with the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRIES RESPECTING MATTERS DISCUSSED AND STATEMENTS MADE

Mr. Chairman, before we pass the supplementary estimate now before us, I would like to make a few remarks concerning the civil service commission.
At this time, French speaking citizens in Canada sometimes wonder about the civil service commission, and the relations which French Canadians may have as federal employees.
I do not consider myself competent to delve very deeply into existing conditions in Ottawa as far as French speaking citizens are concerned. But today I would like to quote as witness a prominent Canadian politician who certainly occupies one of the most important posts in the federal capital. I refer to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) who, as we know, has been deputy minister of justice for several years and who is obviously familiar with the attitude of the civil service commission in respect of French speaking civil servants.
The Minister of Justice recently made a speech in Toronto. I would like to read out a few extracts, and then ask the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) four questions with regard to vote le now before us.
The experience gained by the Minister of Justice would clearly warrant that his statement is based on some true facts. According to the Ottawa Journal of March 5, 1964, the minister said this:

Favreau blames civil service for Quebec's "quiet revolution''.

The beginning of the article reads as follows:

Nothing has caused such "strong and deep-rooted frustration in Quebec" than the position of French Canadians in the federal civil service, especially in the departmental headquarters establishments in the national capital.
The "brushing aside" of French in Ottawa has "fed the so-called quiet revolution" in Quebec.

And the article continues as follows:

These and other statements bearing on bilingualism in the civil service were contained in a speech today at the Empire club in Toronto by justice minister Favreau. He spoke of the feeling now existing among French Canadians as "serious and dangerous", and put the blame largely on the language situation in the civil service.

Again, the article continues:

Mr. Favreau's was the strongest attack yet made by any member of the cabinet against what he charged had been years of discrimination against French Canadians in government service.

That is why the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) asked the President of the Privy Council if he was in agreement with the statements made by the Minister of Justice.
Everybody knows that in Quebec, and more particularly during election campaigns, we heard a great deal of talk about the relations between French Canadians and English Canadians and the part which French Canadians are playing in federal politics. Mr. Chairman, I listened carefully a while ago to the Minister of Justice and I must congratulate him for the courage he showed when he made his two speeches, one in Montreal and the other in Toronto. Now, if more speeches like that had been made these past few years, the situation would be less critical today as regards the education system which, at least in the opinion of some previous speakers, would only date back, under its present form in the province of Quebec, to 1960.
Let me tell you that we, in the province of Quebec, have been striving for a long time to achieve as high a degree of bilingualism as we could wish for and that the system of education was changed, not in 1960, but long before that, for, when I started teaching in 1956, the new system had been in force for eight years. Therefore, it is not the business of the provincial Liberal party of 1960, and this is nothing new, because the province of Quebec was already aware that a change was called for. There were tentative efforts, upheavals, changes, and changes are still being made, but at least we had the courage to 20220-111
Supply-Secretary of State change and to depart somewhat from our traditions, by learning a language and discarding the rest.
If we make the effort to learn another language, it is because we believe it might prove useful to us, otherwise we would not take the trouble. The Canadian people is fully aware of this and I think it is time parliament also understood that as long as a second language is learned only for learning's sake, there shall never be any true bilingualism in the federal civil service. The person who speaks both languages fluently has not only an additional asset, but if he is working in the civil service, he gives double satisfaction. When it is recognized that a knowledge of both languages is an asset, that a bilingual person possesses supplementary or superior qualifications compared with the person who knows only one language, allowance being made for basic qualifications, only then will we have real bilingualism at the level of the civil service.
When an industry needs a technician or an engineer, it does not look for it in a school of medicine but in an institute of technology. If a student wants to specialize in commercial sciences, he attends the school of higher commercial studies and if he wants to be a doctor, he goes to the faculty of medicine.
Now, if the federal government wants efficient men in the civil service, if it wants a team of competent men, it should first have a plan and set up a school to teach and guide the civil service people, in order that they may become efficient men. Many promises were made in that respect during the last election campaign. If the Minister of Justice or the Secretary of State did not make those promises themselves, I heard them say in my riding that a bonus would be granted all bilingual civil servants.
Let the government keep its promises and do what it says it will do. If a person makes the effort required to learn a second language in order to be of service to the federal government, the person should be paid for that service. That should in no way amount to discrimination against other people, for anyone remains free to learn a second language, be it French or English.
I feel it is time we begin to appreciate at its proper value the knowledge of a person who is perfectly bilingual and serves his country in its two official languages.
It is up to the federal government to recognize that advantage. Much ground has already been covered. We are not blaming English speaking Canada, but we rather blame the Quebec representatives within the federal government who, for years and

Supply-Secretary of State years, were rather unconcerned and when I say that, the Minister of Justice knows very well what I am trying to imply.

Now, it is up to this government to take a decision because if the province of Quebec is changing its education system to meet today's needs, it behooves the federal government to take the necessary steps to keep pace with the facts.
And only then may we say that we have qualified civil servants because they will have studied to become fluent in both languages.
If I wished to learn mathematics, I would attend a school where mathematics are taught. The federal government should establish a school of languages in order to provide this service to civil servants. It should improve the knowledge of its employees in order that they may give the best possible service to the Canadian people.
I think that by giving a bonus to those who speak both languages, many federal civil servants would learn the other language and thus they would be in a position to render greater services not only to the civil service commission, but also to the whole Canadian population.

Mr. Chairman, before item le is carried, I would have a brief comment to make.
I refer to a fact concerning the civil service commission to which I drew the attention of the responsible minister twice during the last session.
The civil service commission has advertised job opportunities in a town located in my constituency, the town of Chibougamau. On the posters the citizens of Chibougamau as well as those in the Lake St. John area are asked to submit application forms. 25e. To sustain technological capability in Canadian industry by supporting selected defence development programs, on terms and conditions approved by treasury board, $5,500,000.

Perhaps the minister could give us an explanation of this item. I think I know what the explanation may be. I take it these are moneys which we are advancing from time to time to certain companies producing for national defence in order to assist in industrial development in this field. I wonder whether the minister would confirm the explanation of this item and also perhaps for a minute-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Thirty seconds.
Someone says 30 seconds but we will say a minute-give us the results that are accruing from these expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take it the hon. member has reference to vote 25e. The main estimates contained an appropriation of $10 million to sustain technological capability in Canadian industry by supporting selected

Supply-Defence Production defence development programs. Under this item a forecast is made of development programs which have a likelihood of success and a forecast is made of the amount of success which might be achieved during the year. From time to time Canada is fortunate in having success achieved more rapidly than we had hoped, in which case a higher expenditure than originally forecast is needed.
This supplementary estimate of $5 million does represent a measure of the successful acceleration of our development programs. If it would help the hon. member and the committee I might mention some of these by way of example. One of the larger ones has been the Caribou II aircraft, a project undertaken for the development of a short range take-off and landing aircraft with a military application, in which a great deal of interest has already been shown by the United States army. Hon. members will recollect that for a while it looked as if the United States would not continue its interest in this aircraft, but I am glad to say that the interest has been resumed.
Another one is the development, in conjunction with some of our NATO partners in Europe, notably the United Kingdom, of a drone known as the CL-89 being developed at Canadair for battlefield surveillance. This is coming ahead very satisfactorily indeed. Another example would be the integrated guidance system being developed in Ottawa by Computing Devices Limited.
I could go on and cite other examples which I would suggest are testimony to the ingenuity, perseverance and technological capability of Canadian industry in developing these new devices for the armed forces.

Mr. Chairman, there is only one matter I want to deal with particularly. In his concluding words the minister paid a compliment to the technological development of Canada after having referred to the interest of the United States in the Caribou II. I am wondering why it was that the Royal Canadian Air Force decided to buy Hercules transport aircraft in the United States to the number of 16, as I recall, rather than doing something to make this $55 million order available to Canadian industry. Is there not an aircraft industry in the city of Montreal that could have provided transports sufficient for Canada's purposes? Certainly a boost of $55 million in orders would have given a tremendous impetus to the aircraft industry of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no question but that the aircraft industry in Montreal is fully capable of producing 16 aircraft of the kind required by the Royal Canadian Air Force for transport purposes. However, the

cost of the taxpayers of Canada would have been very substantial indeed in comparison with the cost of buying them from an existing operating assembly line in Georgia. Consequently the decision was taken to purchase them at a substantially lower cost in the United States.
While on the face of it this may seem to represent a lot of job opportunities in the aircraft plant in Montreal, I recall to the house that the defence production sharing program is designed to take care of situations precisely such as this whereby, as a counterpart to Canada being free to purchase its limited requirements of any given item of equipment in the United States, the United States for its part will make purchases from Canada of a corresponding value of military equipment from Canadian manufacturing plants. Canadair in Montreal, to which reference has been made, has been favoured in this production sharing program to a very large degree, particularly in respect of the CF-104 interceptor aircraft, amongst other things.
It may interest the right hon. gentleman to know that at the moment, with this production sharing arrangement of a two way flow of the procurement of military equipment, the balance in favour of Canada is something of the order of $70 million. While it is true that the recent order for Hercules aircraft does represent a substantial purchase in the United States, we will see that this is adequately compensated for by purchases by the United States or on behalf of the United States armed forces from Canadian manufacturers.

I realize, as the minister has said, that defence production sharing is a two way street, but when we were in office we greatly increased the favourable amount of expenditure for Canada. However, I would have thought that on a matter such as this Canada could very well have filled this order and that the fullest consideration should have been given to the merits of the matter.
The minister says that the cost of these aircraft was much lower than would have been the case if similar transport aircraft had been purchased from Canadair. Having said that, I suggest he allow the house and the country to know what was the amount per unit which was asked for a Canadian transport aircraft by Canadian industry. We found ourselves in that position on occasion when military requirements produced in Canada would have cost so much more than almost equally good equipment which could be purchased elsewhere that, in the general picture of defence sharing, orders were given abroad.
However, I should like to hear the actual story from the minister, who is fully conversant with this matter. It is only in the

last few days that I have received the strongest protests from Montreal in this regard. Indeed these protests have come from persons who are quite close to the minister and who found it difficult to understand why an order such as this went elsewhere, when transports could have been provided in Montreal that would have assured the preservation and expansion of the aircraft industry. There is nothing more difficult today than the maintenance of the aircraft industry, as the minister knows. In the United States, I speak from recollection only, I believe there are only three major aircraft concerns left today. The others have had to close down or join the existing ones. Canadian aircraft produced by this country have had a superb performance record and represented the highest of our Canadian technology. I should like the minister to give us the facts rather than the general conclusions that he has given us.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
In respect of the particular aircraft in question, the Hercules aircraft, the difference in cost between having the 16 purchased in Montreal rather than purchased at the Lockheed Corporation in the United States, would have been about $2 million per aircraft or a total of $32 million extra. To pursue this particular line of endeavour at exorbitant cost, to engage in uneconomic operations, to fly in the face of our argument in favour of the rationalization of defence industry with the United States, would possibly have led to a serious breach in the understanding we hope will be reached whereby Canadair will be producing, as part of the production sharing arrangements, components and substantial parts of the TFX aircraft which, as the hon. gentleman knows, is going to be ordered in substantial numbers by the United States air force.
If the position of the Canadian government should be that we are going to produce all our own military equipment, even on an uneconomic basis, then the willingness of the United States to have us share in the production of their military equipment, notably the TFX, I think would be seriously prejudiced. I am quite sure the right hon. gentleman would not wish this to happen. I have given an indication of the magnitude of the uneconomic nature of this operation. In my opinion it would not make sense for us to engage in an uneconomic operation when we can secure the aircraft at a lower cost and at the same time have the equivalent U.S. expenditures made in Canada.

There is just one more question in connection with the figure given by the minister, the $2 million more per unit.
Supply-Defence Production Was the minister referring to Caribou II aircraft in that price, or was he referring to the Hercules?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The Hercules.
Would not the Caribou II have been sufficient for the Canadian air force, and what would have been the cost of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: No; the Caribou aircraft is completely different and designed for a completely different purpose. What the Royal Canadian Air Force is seeking and needs is a long range, high speed, large capacity transport aircraft. These are not the characteristics of the Caribou II. The outstanding feature of it is the short take-off and landing, but a limited range and, by comparison with the Hercules, a very limited capacity.

Mr. Chairman, I only have one question to ask the Minister of Industry and Defence Production. Following the decision taken by Trans-Canada Air Lines to buy American aircraft, can the minister tell the house what will be the value in dollars and cents of the parts which will be manufactured in Canadian aircraft factories, such as Canadair, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: If the hon. member does not mind, I shall reply in English. The arrangements between Douglas Aircraft in the United States and de Havilland in Toronto with respect to the DC-9 aircraft, which is the one under discussion, provide that total purchases from de Havilland Aircraft in Canada may well exceed the total cost of the aircraft being bought by Air Canada for its purposes. If the DC-9 goes as well as it is hoped, it is likely the total expenditures by Douglas at de Havilland will be greater than the total purchase price paid by Air Canada for the aircraft required.
A supplementary question, Mr. Chairman. Can the minister tell the house what amount of money will be spent at Canadair, should certain parts be made there? [Text]

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, there are some subcontracts from de Havilland to Canadair with respect to the DC-9, but I am sorry I do not know precisely what they are.

Could the minister give us any definite estimate as to what amount of money we can expect from the United States? It is all very well for him to say it may exceed the purchase amount involved, but this will

Supply-Defence Production not satisfy the people in Montreal working for Canadair or for the other aircraft companies. We want something definite. I think it would not be too much trouble for him to give these figures, and we shall be lenient with respect to a differential of 5 or 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Unfortunately the hon. gentleman is asking me to forecast the future sales throughout the world of the DC-9. I think he will recognize it would be imprudent for me to engage in that kind of crystal ball gazing.

35e. Canadian Arsenals Limited-administration and operation, $501,100.

Mr. Chairman, the people of St. Paul l'Ermite are now very worried about the fate of the Canadian Arsenals plant, where a number of employees have been laid off.
Can the minister tell the house whether he anticipates an increase in the work force in that plant at a future date, following possible contracts obtained in the United States or in Canada?
I also want to ask the minister whether there is a possibility of reviewing the agreements between the municipality of St. Paul 1'Ermite and the federal government in respect of the grants the latter is paying the municipality in lieu of school and municipal taxes. The responsibilities of the municipality of St. Paul l'Ermite have been increasing constantly, and it would be important to review the arrangement and raise the federal grants in lieu of school and municipal taxes.
I would be grateful to the minister if he would answer the first part of my question and tell me whether he intends trying to obtain rather big contracts large enough so that the work force would be increased, instead of being reduced as it is now the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
In response to the first part of the question, the only possible client of Canadian Arsenals is the Department of National Defence. The United States is quite firm that it will not contemplate placing orders with Canadian Arsenals when its own arsenals, like ours, are being under used and under employed.
I would be misleading the hon. member if I were to suggest that it appears from the white paper that the position of Canadian Arsenals in the near future will substantially increase its work, particularly the kind carried out at St. Paul l'Ermite, which has reference to filling of fixed round ammunition. It is unlikely this is going to increase substantially in the future. In response to the


second part of the question I shall be glad to look into the matter of the grant in lieu of taxes paid by Canadian Arsenals to the municipality.

Mr. Chairman, just like in Quebec city, there is in my riding a plant of the Canadian Arsenals Company Limited, and I think that the same problems arise there as throughout the province, if not throughout the country.
Could the minister inform the house whether the supplementary estimates of the Canadian Arsenals, and more especially their administrative and operational costs, include the tenders called for the sale of those plants, since it is widely rumoured that the plants in Quebec city and Valcartier will be put up for sale, to be operated by private enterprise as manufacturers of ammunition and other commodities?
Would the minister tell us therefore whether the amount of $501,100 includes the disposal costs of the Quebec city and Valcartier plants? [Text]

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is a proposal to dispose of the plant at Valcartier but there is not at the moment a proposal to dispose of the plant at Louise basin in Quebec. As the hon. gentleman knows, the so-called citadel plant on Palace hill has now been closed down and in the not too distant future will be disposed of, but in so far as the hon. member has referred to the plant in Louise basin, this will be retained by Canadian Arsenals. Included in the supplementary estimates, vote 35e, are funds required for the administration of Canadian Arsenals, which include the operations to which I have made reference.
Is there anything under this item for the storage and maintenance by Canadian Arsenals of the Bomarc missiles?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The upkeep of the Bomarc missiles is the responsibility in situ of the K.C.A.F. and not of Canadian Arsenals.
Do we keep a storage of spares in the Canadian Arsenals set up?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

le. Departmental administration, $61,900.

Mr. Chairman, there are many things one can say about finance but I am not so sure this is the time to say them. Most of them have been said during the past week, and the minister is not here at the moment. We understand why he is not here because of the load he has been carrying, and it is perhaps just as well he was not in the house

to hear some of the kindly comments made about the way the affairs of the department were administered, which resulted in the situation we found ourselves in yesterday, and which I understand is not yet solved.
I am not sure whether there is an appropriations bill coming up this afternoon or not, but we were told yesterday one was imminent, or coming over the horizon, with respect to the unemployment insurance fund.
Under this vote we have professional and special services, and I would ask the parliamentary secretary what were the professional and special services amounting to $29,500 as outlined in this item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Professional services consisted of several items. The largest one of them was the firm of James R. Carmichael and Company, engaged to provide a technical review of the existing government workshops and other government services, and this cost $18,000. There was another item for P. Maury Mitchell, $2,500, and Professor Hood was engaged as a special consultant for $2,900, and so on.

As we come to the end of our happy Easter holiday period, I have three good will suggestions to make to the Department of Finance, and if any one of them were adopted it would be in the interest and the welfare of the people of Canada. If I have one minute for each proposition, Mr. Chairman, I think I can confine myself to that time. In the first place I would urge the Department of Finance to take an early look at adopting the well established practice of the United States finance department in exempting from personal income tax the interest portion of mortgage payments on homes. Anybody who has bought or sold a house in Canada must be well acquainted with the fact that the interest portion of the payments for these homes-and most of them are bought on credit-are very heavy and continue for a very long time. The Americans stimulate the home building industry and encourage home building and the establishment of homesteads by this practice of exempting from income tax the interest portion of the mortgage payments. I urge that we consider this.
My second proposition is that Canada should cease to be one of the few remaining countries in the world which has no capital gains tax on stock market speculation profits. The point was urged a week or two ago by my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, and I reiterate it, that we are losing many millions of dollars of revenue which could come to 20220-112
Supply-Finance
us legitimately. This revenue could be obtained were we to impose a capital gains tax on stock market speculation profits.
My third and final proposition is this. I think when we consider the fact that something like 40 cents out of every federal dollar goes to pay either the interest on our federal debt or goes to the amounts that we spend on defence, this is a situation which requires very serious study in depth by us all. We have only to consider the vast amounts of money involved in these two channels of expenditures, and I think if we put our heads together, perhaps in a special committee or in a special review, this would be well worth while; it would perhaps result in substantial savings to the taxpayers. It is a fact that we now spend, just to pay for our federal borrowings, $2 million every day. It is another fact that we spend on defence purposes, when the value of some of these defence purposes is very dubious, $2 million every 12 hours. These are immense expenditures, and if we do not come to grips with this problem and reduce these expenditures I fail to see how we can ever hope to make substantial progress in easing the burden on our taxpayers. These are my three propositions, Mr. Chairman, and I hope the Department of Finance will be good enough to take them into consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will be pleased to bring these matters to the attention of the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) if all the provinces signed with the federal government an agreement to benefit from the municipal loans program. Would the minister tell us if it is true that the auditors of the Department of Finance in Ottawa go through the provinces' books and if he feels that this is interfering in a field which, normally, should come under provincial and not federal jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is speaking to vote 38e, which we have not yet come to. I will attempt to get the information he has asked for and give it to him at that time. If it is not readily available, I will get it after the estimates are concluded and pass it on to him.

30e. Royal Canadian Mint-Administration, operation and maintenance, $128,600.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question on this item. With regard to the Royal Canadian Mint I have found there has been a fairly stabilized vote in the estimates in the years I have been in this house. May I ask just what is meant by this additional vote when it includes an item for "Professional and special services" and an amount of $65,000 for "Express on coin shipments", in view of the fact that in past years this has always been a regularized vote, very rarely requiring a supplementary vote? What is the reason for asking for this amount now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am very pleased to answer this question, Mr. Chairman. With regard to the item for professional and special services, a survey of the mint facilities was carried out by a firm of management consultants, Stevenson and Kellogg Ltd. This is the reason for the additional vote.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask if the report of Stevenson and Kellogg will be filed in this house? This is an administration item, is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is administration.
Will the report on this survey be filed in the house?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. The second question raised by the hon. member concerns the additional cost involved in express on coin shipments. It happened that the mint worked at almost full capacity this year, operating 21 hours a day, and an additional 75 million coins were turned out. The original estimate was based on 325 million coins and actually 400 million coins were turned out during the year. The additional express shipment costs arise from this, as do the additional costs for suppliers for coining and medal work. The extra repairs and upkeep of equipment costs arose because the mint was operating to such a high percentage of capacity.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask whether by any chance the item for supplies for coining and medal work has anything to do with any work for special medallions or coins for the Quebec centennial or the centennial of Canada? Is this included here at all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand it is not, Mr. Chairman. It is simply that there were many more coins turned out during the particular year than had been originally estimated. The original estimate of the number of coins was 325 million; the actual number turned out was 400 million. This is just the additional cost involved.

Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary secretary might express to the governor of the mint, Mr. Parker, and his staff our appreciation for the tremendous load they have carried. This astronomical increase in the production of coins is shown here in the additional express costs, and this additional production was carried out by a mint which was built many, many years ago, is not streamlined and does not have the accommodation for this large production. I think we have in the mint a group of officers and men who deserve the commendation of this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will be pleased to pass that commendation on, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the mint is completely swamped at the present time, particularly in the production of silver dollars which are a commemorative item this year-it is said that the orders will be delayed by at least six months-can the parliamentary secretary indicate whether the Stevenson and Kellogg report into the administration of the mint made a recommendation for new accommodation, and how long is anticipated before this can be completed? Coming from a silver industry community, I would be very happy to see this type of increase continue for many years. The amount of silver being used has warranted an increase in the price of silver, and therefore we are very happy about the situation. But I believe the people in the mint are working under conditions which present an almost impossible task, and it looks as though this is not an extra load but is the normal increase that is taking place across the world in the production of coins. The government should have some plan in this regard and should be prepared to give us some outline of that plan for improving this situation, because it does not amount to an emergency but is a continuing and growing problem that will be with us for some time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the survey carried out this year was in connection with plant and lay-out, for which this additional estimate is being put forward. Many of the recommendations of Stevenson and Kellogg are being carried out in the mint now with regard to the matter of plant and lay-out. The second stage, which is the designing of a new mint, a new operational unit which will have a much higher capacity than the existing mint, is under study at the present time.

I realize the parliamentary secretary may not be able to tell us when, but it seems that no matter what they do with the present facility they will not be able to meet the demand or to keep up with it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand that we will have the report in about six months and that it will take from two to two and a half years to complete the new mint.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter which I have wanted to raise all week and I think this is the best item under which to raise it. I think all Canadians were pleased when the Prime Minister indicated to President Johnson that Canada would be quite willing to help in any way we could in providing assistance to the victims of the earthquake in Alaska. This points up the fact that in Canada we really have no machinery for dealing with civil disasters in our country. In the United States there is established machinery whereby at the request of the governor of a state an area is declared a disaster area, and legislative machinery immediately moves into operation to deal with the emergency situation and to help the victims of the particular disaster. I have long thought that we in Canada ought to have some type of machinery established to deal with civil disasters. I recall the Rimouski fire in Quebec, the Humber flood which affected a large number of people in the suburban areas of 20220-1121
Supply-Finance
metropolitan Toronto, the Red river flood which inundated a good part of the city of Winnipeg and the city of St. Boniface, and other disasters of that type which we had to meet on an ad hoc basis.
It takes a certain amount of time to work out a plan of operation between federal, provincial and municipal authorities, as well as charitable organizations who are willing to help. The Canadian people in all these disasters have been most generous, and the delay has not been anyone's fault. The delay has been occasioned by the fact that we have no legal machinery which automatically moves into operation.
I want to use this item to suggest that the government give consideration to consulting with the provinces with a view to preparing civil disaster legislation, so that when any natural disaster takes place there will be an agreed division and apportionment of the costs between federal, provincial and municipal authorities, making use of the emergency measures organization, the army, the Red Cross, the health organizations, all of whom can move into a disaster area immediately, take up their posts, know what are their responsibilities, know what authority they have, and be able to co-ordinate the efforts of private organizations to deal with the situation.
I am not saying this in any spirit of criticism; we have just never faced up to the problem in this country. I think the government could make a good name for itself as well as serve a very useful function by giving consideration to legislation of this type, and I think the provinces would be very glad to co-operate.
The emergency measures organization, which I personally always thought had some value mainly in the field of civil disaster, has operated very well wherever there has been a situation which required their services. But, of course, they have no authority and can only assist the municipal and provincial authorities. They have no funds at their disposal; they have no legislative authority; and they are greatly hampered in doing the job which I think they could do. I think that what happened in the Alberni valley last week is a very good example of this. The minister of northern affairs, who was given responsibility by the federal government to attend to this matter, has in my opinion, been most assiduous in trying to help, and I think the government has responded so far as it has been able to do so.
Last Sunday I spent the entire day in the Alberni valley visiting Alberni and Port Alberni, and when I returned to the mainland I sent a telegram to the Prime Minister. I am very glad that the troops were moved

Supply-Finance
in and I know that any further assistance, so far as permanent rehabilitation is concerned, depends on an appeal being received from the provincial government. I feel certain that if and when the provincial government makes such an appeal the government of Canada will respond, and I hope they will respond generously.
I want to remind the government that in the Rimouski fire and the Red river flood

I think also in the Humber flood but I am not quite sure about that-persons whose homes were damaged or destroyed were enabled to replace them completely. Even small businessmen were assisted in the restoration of their places of business. But in the Alberni valley the damage will be worse. In the other instances people could claim flood damage, but I am told by some of the insurance adjusters that in the case of the Alberni valley this damage is considered to be caused by a tidal wave and is not covered by the ordinary flood insurance provisions. I do not know whether or not that is correct, but if it is correct it means that these unfortunate people will not even get flood insurance. I think roughly 50 homes were completely demolished, and the estimate I received was that 300 homes were badly damaged. And when these people say "badly" they mean that homes have been moved off their foundations, sometimes toppled over on their ends, all furniture smashed, all bedding, clothing, dishes and utensils rendered useless; so these people are in very difficult circumstances.
It is true that in terms of degree it does not amount to anything like the disaster which has been experienced in Alaska; but for the several hundred families which are directly affected it is a disaster. I have been urging all week that in addition to what the federal government is prepared to do to rehabilitate these people at the request of the government of British Columbia, the government should in the meantime give some serious thought to making a substantial financial contribution to the Alberni valley disaster fund. I think this would do two things. First, it would enable the excellent committee which has been set up to know they have some money behind them, and would enable them to take care of the people who are homeless. The committee has as its honorary chairman the lieutenant governor of the province, and I believe wires have also been sent to the premier of the province and the leader of the opposition to act as honorary vice chairman. The mayors of two cities, Mayor Hammer of Port Alberni and Mayor Bishop of Alberni, have set up an excellent committee; they are getting good co-operation from the emergency measures organization and private organizations like the Salvation Army.

They have a very good welfare officer there from Vancouver and I think they have the machinery to do a very adequate job of looking after those who are homeless. When I left there on Sunday evening there were still 77 families without a roof over their heads. I think some 233 families had been placed with their neighbours and they had some temporary accommodation. But all these families will, when they get back into their homes, require not only the money needed for the rebuilding of those homes but, in addition, all the furniture, bedding and other things which are necessary to set up housekeeping.
I think it would be a tremendous boost to the morale of these people if the government were to announce it would put a very substantial sum into this disaster fund. This would not preclude the government from sitting down later with the government of British Columbia and working out some shared program for the cost of the replacement of these homes and places of business. However, in the meantime, while the British Columbia government is making its survey and getting ready to make its representation to Ottawa, I feel something should be done immediately.
I recognize the minister's difficulty. He cannot intervene in a provincial situation without the consent of the provincial government concerned. But I do not think it requires consent from anyone to make a contribution to a disaster fund. I believe in the old idea that help delayed is virtually help denied and that the sooner we do something, the better.
I would therefore make these two requests to the government: First, that thought be given to enacting some type of civil disaster legislation so that when we face situations of this kind in the future legal machinery will be available whereby the people affected can be cared for expeditiously and effectively. Second, I ask that in this particular instance the government give some thought to making a contribution to the Alberni valley disaster fund, so that these people on the committee may have some money to take care of the immediate situation, pending a report on what must be done to rehabilitate these communities.

May I add a few words to what has been said by my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam? I was a member of the British Columbia legislature at the time of the major flooding of the Fraser river-the most serious floods we have experienced in British Columbia and one of the greatest disasters ever to hit our province. The army and the militia responded to the emergency but the arrangements for taking care of those directly affected were such that, to the best

of my knowledge, it was 18 months or two years before responsibility was accepted and settlements were made.
Once again we have been faced by a major disaster. My reason for wishing to add a few words to what has been said by my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam is that at the time of the flood disaster I was not only a member of the British Columbia house but leader of the opposition, and at that time I made an appeal in the legislature for legislation of exactly the kind my hon. friend is asking for now, that is, the establishment by law of a disaster fund applicable anywhere where the need arises. Why is it that we have to wait year after year, almost decade after decade, before consideration is given to a recommendation of this kind?
I have an additional reason for speaking in support of the appeal which has just been made to the government, and that is the present reported state of the emergency fund. May I direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who is in his place and who has been given authority in this situation, and ask him to tell us the extent of the emergency disaster fund at the present moment? I have recently left our reading room and according to what the Vancouver papers say it consists of $50,000 guaranteed by the premier of British Columbia, $50,000 from a power company and $12,000 from anonymous donations. Thus, according to these newspaper reports, $112,000 is the extent of the disaster fund. Again, if the papers are correct, the damage amounts to an estimated $5 million not including the damage done to industry itself. This situation is pretty darned rotten, when a disaster fund produced by anonymous contributions and two guarantees amounts to $100,000 in the face of a need of that magnitude. No fund, nothing, no direct contribution from the federal government.
I certainly hope the observations of my hon. friend will be heeded. First, a disaster fund should be created, available on call whenever it might be needed and, second, consideration should be given, now, to the immediate provision of necessities by the federal government to those who are in need.

I do not want to review what has already been said. I believe the emergency measures organization is fully effective in carrying out the ordinary duties which follow disasters whenever they may take place. Indeed I recall one or two occasions when the services of that organization were made available and it carried out its responsibilities in a manner which brought honour to all who were engaged. However that is not why I wish to speak.

My observations have to do with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, that the government of Canada might well consider making a contribution to the disaster fund. I feel that action along this line would receive general support in the house and I rise merely to repeat what I have said on earlier occasions in the questions I have asked, namely that anything done by the government in this connection would receive the support of the opposition.
Certainly, the constitutional division of responsibility denies the making of any direct contribution to the areas which have been subject to disaster but I can see no difficulty about a contribution being made to alleviate the conditions under which many families find themselves in the Alberni area. The other day I stated the information I had was that the loss ran into tens of millions of dollars. The minister said the estimate of total damage he had was $5 million. I brought his estimate to the attention of the people who had communicated with me and they told me they thought it was far too low. I recognize, of course, that immediately after a catastrophe strikes the estimates sometimes far exceed what subsequent investigation actually determines the losses to be. Suffice it to say that I wanted to make clear that any assistance given to that' fund will receive our unqualified support.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the first two hon. members who spoke decided to use this item to impress upon the government the advisability of setting up some organization of a permanent nature which would take over automatically in the case of disasters in the country. I think the idea has much to commend it, but I do want to say that in respect of the difficulty in the Alberni valley there has been the closest co-operation and instantaneous action on the part of E.M.O., the Canadian Red Cross, the civil defence organization and various other agencies.
I have attempted to keep in touch as closely as I could with Mayor Hammer and Mayor Bishop of the two cities. After my wire to Hon. W. D. Black on Monday, in which I asked him to furnish us with a copy of the assessment of loss, he advised me that they were holding a cabinet meeting on Thursday and he would get in touch with me immediately thereafter. Yesterday I talked to the two mayors again and asked if in their view it would seem reasonable for us to withhold any decision as to the making of a contribution to the fund until after this meeting of the British Columbia cabinet on Thursday.
I pointed out that if we were making a contribution to the repairing of the damage it

Supply-Finance
would be several times the $50,000 that the province of British Columbia has contributed.
I believe that yesterday the provincial cabinet appointed a firm of insurance adjusters, E. A. Earl and Associates of Vancouver, who have been asked to make an assessment of the damage and to report to the government in one week, so that from the viewpoint of our participation the matter apparently has been delayed a week. I want to tell hon. members that if we are not called upon to participate in the ordinary course of events, with the province in the rehabilitation, I will have no hesitation in recommending to my colleagues that a very substantial contribution be made to the disaster fund, but I rather expect that we may be asked to participate in the rehabilitation of the community as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to belabour this point or delay the committee, except to make one observation about the minister's remarks. I quite agree with what both he and the Leader of the Opposition have said about the emergency measures organization being most effective and most helpful. I had the privilege on Sunday afternoon of sitting in on a meeting chaired by the two mayors, which was attended by representatives of all organizations, including a representative from the emergency measures organization, and I quite agree that E.M.O. can serve a useful purpose in co-ordinating the efforts of the different groups.
This does not alter the fact that neither E.M.O. nor anyone else there had the authority to spend one red cent. A representative was there from the department of social welfare and he said, "I have no authority". The two mayors said, "We have no money". The Red Cross and the Salvation Army were the only two groups which said that they had received some authority from their national organizations and could spend up to X thousand dollars, neither of which amounts, or both together, would be enough to make a reasonable approach to the problem, let alone solve it.
I am not suggesting that legislation be brought down to set up a permanent organization. What I am suggesting is that we set up legislative authority so that when, on the request of a provincial premier, an area is declared a disaster area the federal government will be authorized to move in troops or engineers where necessary, and so that funds will automatically be available on some prearranged percentage basis. In this way the committee which is established including a federal representative, a provincial representative and a municipal representative will know that they can proceed immediately to
[Mr. Laing.l
buy clothing, bedding, and whatever equipment they need to take care of destitute people.
That is my real concern, and I point out that there is still nothing being done about it. When you go to visit a home, as I did, and see six or eight inches of mud on the floor, all the furniture overturned, the house sitting at an angle of 45 degrees and the man and woman who have been up all night trying to bail out the water and shovel out the mud while having no place to sleep, and not even being able to prepare a meal for themselves, then it is not enough to say that in a week or two the governments will get together and do something about it. What I am pleading for is the kind of machinery under which organizations can move into an area knowing that they can draw on the federal and provincial treasuries for some stipulated amount of money which would have to be accounted for, but which could be used immediately to set up outdoor kitchens and emergency shelter, so that people who are in dire circumstances will not be allowed to go in want.
We have had a number of disasters in Canada and it would be very interesting to trace how many funds were set up and where those funds are today. In the case of many of these funds there was a residue, after everything had been taken care of, and the money is lying somewhere; but before you can spend that money you have to find the trustees of the fund, which is not easy. If we had some sort of national organization set up and funds were raised, then anything that was left over after a particular disaster had been taken care of would revert to the fund and would be available for use in the next disaster. We would always have some money on hand and those charged with the responsibility of trying to render help in an emergency would know that those funds were available. This is what I am pleading for and I hope the government will give some thought to it.

Mr. Chairman, my comments on the Department of Justice will have to be, not in poetry but in the more usual form of prose. Inasmuch as this item involves a grant to the Canadian corrections association to assist in defraying the expenses of the fifth international criminological congress to be held in Montreal in 1965, I should like to make some comments about the general question of criminological procedures and to express my regret that because of a sort of parting gift by the former minister of justice, all the background policy and previous attitude of the government, and certainly of the former Conservative government when the department was headed by Mr. Fulton, seem to have been wiped out to satisfy a political promise.
I know that this may upset some people in Cornwall, but I just do not think that Cornwall is the place to put the new prison for women. Anybody who has paid any attention to criminological or sociological matters is of the opinion that penitentiaries and prisons should be placed in those areas where sociologists, criminologists and people interested in this field can have easy access to these institutions in order to work with the prison officials, and particularly the inmates, from the point of view of bringing about their rehabilitation. As far as I am concerned, the decision to build the new prison for women at Cornwall detracts from any such program.
Anybody who has been through the existing women's prison at Kingston will certainly agree that it is an antiquated and disgraceful structure, in which nothing useful is accomplished outside of locking people behind doors, and that there is certainly a need for a new prison. But in my view the new prison for women should be constructed within the complex that exists at Kingston, rather than being transplanted to some part of the country removed from the benefit of all the good work that can be done by people from Queen's

Supply-Justice
University, and those in the penitentiaries branch who are already working in the Kingston complex.
I also wish to express some concern about the proposed drug treatment centre at Matsqui. After my national leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and I visited the B.C. penitentiary last winter I drove up the Fraser valley to Matsqui the following day to look at the situation. The ground is levelled off and there is a nice wire fence around the property in preparation for the establishment of this new so-called drug treatment centre. But so far I have not heard a single word from anybody in the government with regard to just what is supposed to take place at that centre. The government seems to have no policy and no ideas with regard to rehabilitation from a clinical or sociological point of view.
If nothing more is going to be done in dealing with people addicted to narcotics than has been done in the past, then to all intents and purposes the $7| million or whatever the amount is that is going to be spent at Matsqui is a waste of money. I say that because all we will be building is another prison in which we can lock up people and, when their time is up, open the doors and let them out again so they can start the whole process all over again of looking for drugs, being apprehended and tossed into jail once more. This is what we have been doing in Canada for years, and so far we have achieved absolutely nothing except to fill our prisons- in the west in any event, where there is a high incidence of narcotic addiction-with people who are unfortunately addicted to narcotics.
We have not turned a single stone in the field of so-called drug treatment. We have not heard a word in this regard from this government, its predecessors or from the provincial government of British Columbia which is concerned with the general question of health. We have had nothing but the following of procedures used in the United States, which have been an abject failure if anything has. While we are not taking action under this item, I say that before we blindly proceed to endorse the building of another prison complex at Matsqui and give it the fancy name of a drug treatment centre, we had better ask some searching questions and get some sensible, farsighted answers from the government as to just what it intends to accomplish and how it intends to proceed at this drug treatment centre. If we do not do so we will just be spending another $7J million or $8 million on another prison which will accomplish precisely the same thing in the field of drug treatment that prisons have accomplished in the past-absolutely nothing.

Mr. Chairman, we are spending this $10,000 to have the fifth international criminological congress held in Canada in 1965. Unless the Department of Justice comes up with something worth while I should think we should be ashamed to have this congress meet in Canada. We are very far behind in penal reform. As the hon. member for Skeena has mentioned, we have built prisons to contain people, rather than correctional institutions to help to rehabilitate them.
In my own small way I have examined several aspects of this problem and I find that the new states of Alaska and Mexico, and other countries, have made much more progress than we have. In some cases they have not had the benefit of a royal commission report, such as that of the Fauteux commission, but yet we have done very little by way of reform to make us proud of what we have accomplished in Canada. Since this congress is meeting in Canada I would think we would want to be able to show other nations the advances we have made, but the fact is that in the whole field of justice there is very little in this country of which we can be proud. Certainly this is true when you find the province of Ontario putting through a bill such as was introduced in the legislature a few weeks ago.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the Department of Justice could at least pick one field and concentrate on it, so that we would be able to have something to show the congress with regard to the advances that are possible in Canada in the correction of criminals. If we picked one field we should at least be able to give some leadership to the congress in that field. Canada is not such a backward country that we cannot pick out and concentrate on making advances in one field. In this way we would be able to show the delegates who will be attending the congress that there is at least one aspect of criminology in which we are better than other countries.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let this item go by without making a brief comment on it. We have waited a reasonable length of time, being reasonable people, and I should now like to ask the parliamentary secretary-I believe the Minister of Justice is unavoidably absent-whether the government has definitely decided to move the women's prison from Kingston to Cornwall. A good many people in my district who work at the prison are naturally much concerned about this decision. They are people who have put down their roots in the district through purchasing modest though comfortable homes, and they want to know what the future has

in store for them. The interests of these people should be considered.
Then again, the various associations of social workers throughout the district are protesting this pending move. I wish to point out, as has been done before, that Queen's University is well equipped to treat these inmates from a social or psychological aspect. We have two good hospitals in the area that are well equipped to handle any emergency. They are the Kingston General hospital and Hotel Dieu, both well equipped and staffed, and both of which are expanding. I would say to the parliamentary secretary, who represents the Department of Justice here, that he should think twice before making a move of this kind. We in the bay of Quinte district are very much concerned about it.
Second, Mr. Chairman, I should like to know if the Department of Justice has abandoned the tenders system in connection with the purchase of beef on the hoof for the penitentiaries at Kingston and Joyceville. I have been told, without any personal inquiry on my part, by the producers of this type of beef that they no longer are invited to tender. These tender forms are no longer mailed out to them. What is going on under this new administration which was going to introduce a new era of service to the public? I ask the question, have you abandoned the tenders system? The supplying of this material now goes to one or two people, no doubt some of your own pets. I would admonish the government to get back to the good tenders system that we used to have in 1962, under which the penitentiaries received good beef at a fair price, and all producers had an opportunity to sell their beef.
Third, Mr. Chairman, although I deplore the necessity of more prisons in this country, I must say I welcome the announcement made the other day by the hon. member for Kingston that a new prison would be constructed. He did not say it would be constructed in Prince Edward-Lennox, but he said it would be at Millhaven. He might more correctly have said at Bath, Ontario, in Prince Edward-Lennox, which is the constituency I represent. The present administration is not the author of this plan. It dates back to the former administration which was studying decentralization of the prison system as long ago as 1959. This announcement is the fruition of the plan. As its representative in the house in the last two parliaments, I have been lauding the merits and the advantages of the location of Prince Edward-Lennox. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that Prince Edward-Lennox accepts the trust that has been laid on its shoulders. We will work with the rest of Canada in the best interests of the

I am somewhat amazed at the discussion that has taken place under this supplementary item. In view of what has been said, therefore, I should like to add a few words of my own.
First of all, with regard to the women's penitentiary, I may say that if hon. members who have spoken within recent minutes were here when I asked a question on orders of the day they would remember I asked the Minister of Justice whether or not the previous minister told the truth or lied when he made a public statement that it was to be moved to Cornwall. The answer I received was, "I will have to take this as notice". Another question I asked was whether or not any decision had been made. The answer was, "Put the question on the order paper". Obviously no definite decision has been made.
What does surprise me, sir, is the remark made by one of my own colleagues in my own party, and the hon. member who just resumed his seat, concerning the relationship between the women's penitentiary in Kingston and Queen's University. I wonder if both hon. members know what the dickens they are talking about. What is the relationship between Queen's University and the women's penitentiary in Kingston, and what has that to do with whether or not the penitentiary should be kept in Kingston? If my information is correct, and I am sure it is, Queen's University does not have a psychiatric department in its medical school. What is the relationship, then, on the basis of psychiatry, between Queen's University and whether or not there will be a women's penitentiary at Kingston? So far as I am concerned, it is very clear, and I have been interested in penology for 30 years. The important consideration is not the location but the job that can be done. When I first heard

Supply-Justice
there was a probability of a new penitentiary being built away from Kingston, I made inquiries. There was talk of Cornwall being the site, and I found that one month ago there was only one woman from Cornwall in the Kingston's women's penitentiary.
I disagree with the construction of a new narcotics centre in the Fraser valley, but if it goes ahead it will mean that one third of those now serving in Kingston penitentiary, the third who are narcotic addicts, will be transferred to the Fraser valley. Of the balance of those now in Kingston one third come from Ontario and Quebec, and one third from the western provinces, and almost all of those from B.C. will be transferred to the narcotics centre in the Fraser valley.
I regret very much that parochialism should be the deciding factor in the location of an institution. I have heard it said this was to be done on a patronage basis, so I made inquiries and I found that in none of the areas suggested yet has the federal government any property, nor has it taken option on any property for the establishment of a women's penitentiary. Therefore when members get up, whether they be from my own party or otherwise, I hope they will realize what they are talking about.
Do not tell me about Queen's University in relation to a penitentiary because it has not got any department of psychiatry or psychology, and do not tell me about patronage when there is no government owned land or government opted land. We are greatly behind in meeting the need for a new women's penitentiary, but it should be established on the right basis of modern penology.
I agree completely with the hon. member for Skeena in his remarks about the $4 million or $5 million narcotics centre in B.C., because it cannot do the job. Such a centre is years behind modern understanding and, as the hon. member for Skeena said, what we are doing is putting up a new prison, and treating addicts as criminals instead of sick people, as they are recognized to be throughout the rest of the world. Both the federal and provincial governments would save millions of dollars if we treated them as sick people and not as criminals.
I did not know that this supplementary estimate would lead us into such a discussion, but I do hope questions of parochialism and provincialism will be set aside and we shall consider the matter on the principles of modern penology and criminology rather than on the proposition of constituency expediency.
